name: Tooth jewelry / gems

lead: Tooth jewelry is a small gem, rhinestone or stud attached to a tooth, usually a front tooth, as a decorative accent. Wearers use it to add sparkle to their smile as a form of personal style.

It is typically bonded to the enamel surface. A case report on a patient with white spot lesions found the patient preferred tooth jewelry as an esthetic option, and a Nigerian case report notes it boosts appearance and confidence [1][2].

paras: A gem is attached with dental adhesive to the outer tooth surface, and is removed by a dental professional or eventually falls off. It is often placed on an upper front tooth or canine.

Case reports describe a child whose stick-on rhinestone embedded in a tooth fractured it and led to tooth loss, and authors discuss health implications for vulnerable populations [3][1]. Dental writers have called for guidance about oral body modification risks.

angle.text: A bonded gem draws attention to the smile as a fashion accent. One case report used it to visually mask white spot lesions without removing tooth structure [2].

lead: Tooth jewelry is the practice of attaching decorative ornaments such as crystals, rhinestones or small studs to teeth. It is a form of oral body modification used for the appearance of the smile.

A 2023 case report from Nigeria states that tooth jewelry boosts appearance and confidence but may carry adverse health consequences [1]. A 2012 case report described using tooth jewelry as a non-destructive way to mask white spot lesions and noted patients' esthetic preference for it [2]. Reports also describe the practice in rural Cambodia and discuss ethical questions for dentists [3][4].

paras: Ornaments are crystals, rhinestones or studs affixed to teeth for decoration. They are one of several perioral and oral body modifications that increased in frequency over about three decades before 2012 [5].

Authors report that wearers seek the look for appearance and confidence [1]. A case report on white spot lesions found that patients preferred tooth jewelry as an esthetic concern and a noninvasive masking option [2].

In a case report of an 8-year-old, a stick-on rhinestone embedded in a tooth for esthetics fractured the tooth and led to its loss; the authors recommend anticipatory guidance about oral modification risks for children, adolescents and adults [5].

The Nigerian case report describes adverse health consequences and a need for appropriate measures to quantify and address the practice [1]. A 2001 South African article framed piercing and tooth jewelry as an ethical dilemma for dentists [4].
No studies found. The literature consists of case reports and letters [1][2][5][3].
